title: Body Plan, Cavities & Fascia
summary: Learn the trunk's map: its planes, cavities, serous linings, fascial layers and surface landmarks that every later lesson builds on.

lessons.title: Anatomical Position, Planes and Regions of the Trunk

levels.kid:
Imagine everyone used a different map of the body. One doctor says "left," another means a different left. Total confusion! So doctors agreed on one starting pose, called **anatomical position**. You stand up straight, look forward, arms at your sides, palms facing forward.

Then they slice the body with pretend sheets of glass. One sheet cuts you into left and right. One cuts you into front and back. One cuts you into top and bottom.

Your tummy gets a map too. Doctors draw a tic-tac-toe grid on it, making **nine squares**. If your tummy hurts in the bottom right square, the doctor knows where to look. It's like a treasure map for your insides!
levels.hs:
Anatomists describe the body from one standard pose, **anatomical position**: standing upright, head and eyes facing forward, arms at the sides with palms facing forward, feet together. "Left" and "right" always mean the patient's left and right, not the viewer's.

Three kinds of **planes** cut through the body:
- **Sagittal** planes divide it into left and right parts. The **median (midsagittal)** plane runs down the exact middle.
- **Coronal (frontal)** planes divide it into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts.
- **Transverse (axial)** planes divide it into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts. CT scans show the body in this view.

Direction words come in pairs: **anterior/posterior**, **superior/inferior**, **medial/lateral** (toward or away from the midline), and **superficial/deep**.

The abdomen is mapped in two ways:
- **Four quadrants**, made by the median plane and a horizontal line through the umbilicus (belly button): right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower.
- **Nine regions**, made by two vertical lines and two horizontal lines.

Real example: a patient with appendicitis often feels pain that starts near the umbilicus and moves to the **right lower quadrant**, where the appendix usually lies. Using shared terms lets every clinician picture the same spot instantly.
levels.college:
**Anatomical position** is the reference frame for all descriptions: body erect, face and gaze forward, upper limbs at the sides with palms anterior, lower limbs together with toes forward. Descriptions hold even when the patient is supine or prone, because terms refer to this position, not the actual posture.

**Planes**
- **Median plane**: a single vertical plane through the midline. Parallel **sagittal (parasagittal)** planes lie lateral to it.
- **Coronal planes**: vertical, at right angles to the median plane.
- **Transverse (axial/horizontal) planes**: at right angles to both. Radiology shows axial slices as if viewed from the patient's feet, so the patient's right appears on the viewer's left.

**Relational terms**: superior/inferior (cranial/caudal), anterior/posterior (ventral/dorsal), medial/lateral, proximal/distal, superficial/deep, and **ipsilateral/contralateral**.

**Regions of the trunk**: the trunk is the thorax, abdomen and pelvis. The thorax is subdivided clinically into the pectoral, sternal and axillary regions on the front, and the scapular and vertebral regions on the back.

**Abdominal subdivision**
- **Quadrants**: the median plane plus the **transumbilical plane** (usually near the L3/L4 disc). These are simple and preferred at the bedside.
- **Nine regions**: two **midclavicular planes** (vertical), the **subcostal plane** (upper horizontal) and the **intertubercular (transtubercular) plane** (lower horizontal). Some texts use the transpyloric and interspinous planes instead.
  - Top row: right hypochondrium, **epigastric**, left hypochondrium.
  - Middle row: right flank (lumbar), **umbilical**, left flank.
  - Bottom row: right groin (inguinal/iliac), **pubic (hypogastric)**, left groin.

Organ projections guide examination. The liver and gallbladder project to the right hypochondrium. The spleen projects to the left hypochondrium. The appendix projects to the right groin, and the sigmoid colon to the left groin. These maps are approximate, because organs shift with breathing, posture and body build.
levels.phd:
Anatomical terminology is codified in **Terminologia Anatomica** (TA, 1998; TA2, 2019), produced by FIPAT under the IFAA. It replaced the earlier Nomina Anatomica lineage that began with the Basle Nomina Anatomica of 1895. TA standardizes plane and region names. For example, it lists the nine abdominal regions as hypochondriac, epigastric, lateral (flank), umbilical, inguinal and pubic. It also prefers "pubic region" over "hypogastrium," though both remain in clinical use.

The **nine-region scheme** is not uniformly defined. The lower horizontal plane may be the intertubercular plane, through the tubercles of the iliac crests at about L5, or the interspinous plane, through the anterior superior iliac spines. The upper plane may be the subcostal plane, at the lowest point of the costal margin (10th costal cartilage, near L3), or the transpyloric plane. Because definitions differ, the same organ may be assigned to different regions in different textbooks. This is a quiet source of confusion in teaching.

Directional terms carry assumptions from comparative anatomy. In bipeds, "ventral" and "anterior" coincide, as do "cranial" and "superior." In quadrupeds they do not, which is why veterinary and embryological texts prefer cranial/caudal and dorsal/ventral. Embryology adds rostral, used for the neural axis, which bends at the cephalic flexure. The trunk's longitudinal axis therefore aligns cleanly with the neuraxis, but the forebrain does not.

Imaging conventions are themselves standards. Axial CT and MRI are displayed viewed from below with the patient supine, so anterior is at the top of the image. Coronal images are displayed as if facing the patient. In a supine patient, gravity changes organ positions relative to these planes. Classic cadaver-based surface projections came from embalmed, supine specimens. Studies of living subjects using CT, such as Mirjalili and colleagues' work (2012) re-examining surface anatomy, showed many traditional projections to be inaccurate in living, upright people. Viscera sit lower when upright and vary with body habitus. Regions are therefore probabilistic maps, not fixed addresses.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the quadrant and region language matters less as anatomy than as a way of describing pain and handing over information. Several pitfalls follow.

**Visceral vs somatic localization.** Early visceral pain is felt in the midline according to embryological origin, not organ position. Foregut pain is felt epigastrically, midgut pain periumbilically, and hindgut pain suprapubically. This is why appendicitis begins periumbilically. Only when the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed does pain localize to the right lower quadrant, near **McBurney's point**. The point lies one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. A region therefore tells you where the patient feels pain, which only partly overlaps with where the organ lies.

**Variation in position.** Pregnancy displaces the appendix upward. A retrocecal appendix may produce flank or back pain. Situs inversus mirrors the whole map. Elderly and obese patients may localize poorly. A good habit is to document the precise point and the radiation of pain, not just the quadrant.

**Laterality errors.** The patient's-right rule underlies wrong-side surgery prevention. WHO's Surgical Safety Checklist and the Joint Commission Universal Protocol require site marking for lateralized procedures. Mirror-image imaging displays and prone positioning are known contributors to laterality errors. Neurosurgery, with lateralized spine and cranial work, is a historically high-risk specialty here.

**Imaging-era planes.** Surgeons increasingly think in scanner planes rather than surface regions. Multiplanar and 3D reconstruction now plans port placement, oblique approaches and navigation in true anatomical coordinates. Oblique planes, such as those along the long axis of the heart or kidney, do not fit the classic three-plane system. Specialty-specific axes have grown up to describe them, and cardiology now uses attitudinally correct nomenclature over the traditional "Valentine" orientation.

**Open questions.** Should education adopt living, upright reference anatomy and population-adjusted landmarks over the cadaveric tradition? Data from CT and upright MRI support revising several textbook projections. However, curricula and exams change slowly, so trainees must learn both the conventions and their limits.

keyPoints: Anatomical position: upright, facing forward, palms forward; left/right means the patient's
Sagittal planes split left/right, coronal front/back, transverse top/bottom
Paired terms: anterior/posterior, superior/inferior, medial/lateral, superficial/deep
Four quadrants use the median and transumbilical planes
Nine regions use midclavicular, subcostal and intertubercular planes
Region maps are approximate: organs shift with posture, breathing and build

test.q: In anatomical position, the palms face:
test.explain: Anatomical position has the palms facing anteriorly (forward), with the arms at the sides.

test.q: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
test.explain: Coronal (frontal) planes separate front from back. Sagittal and median planes separate left from right.

test.q: A standard CT scan slice is usually displayed in which plane?
test.explain: CT is classically acquired and shown in transverse (axial) slices, viewed from the patient's feet.

test.q: The four abdominal quadrants are formed by the median plane and the:
test.explain: A horizontal plane through the umbilicus crossed with the median plane makes the four quadrants.

test.q: Which vertical lines form the nine-region grid?
test.explain: Two midclavicular planes are the vertical boundaries of the nine regions.

test.q: The central region of the top row of the nine regions is the:
test.explain: The top row is right hypochondrium, epigastric, then left hypochondrium.

test.q: The spleen projects mainly to which region?
test.explain: The spleen lies under the left costal margin, in the left hypochondrium. The liver occupies the right hypochondrium.

test.q: A structure on the same side of the body as another is described as:
test.explain: Ipsilateral means on the same side. Contralateral means on the opposite side.

test.q: Appendicitis pain classically settles in which quadrant?
test.explain: The appendix usually lies in the right lower quadrant, where localized pain settles.

test.q: The single sagittal plane through the exact midline is called the ___ plane.
test.explain: The median (midsagittal) plane divides the body into equal left and right halves.

test.q: What term means toward the midline of the body?
test.explain: Medial means toward the midline; lateral means away from it.

test.q: The lower horizontal plane of the nine regions passes through the iliac tubercles and is called the ___ plane.
test.explain: The intertubercular plane forms the lower horizontal boundary of the nine regions in the common scheme.

kidTest.q: In anatomical position, which way do your palms face?
kidTest.explain: Palms face forward in the standard pose.

kidTest.q: Why did doctors agree on one starting pose?
choices: So everyone uses the same map
kidTest.explain: One shared pose means left, right, front and back mean the same thing to everyone.

kidTest.q: How many squares are in the tummy grid?
kidTest.explain: Two up-and-down lines and two across lines make nine squares.

kidTest.q: One pretend glass sheet cuts you into left and right. Another cuts you into front and:
kidTest.explain: Doctors use sheets that cut left/right, front/back and top/bottom.

kidTest.q: The tummy grid works like a treasure m _ _ for your insides.
kidTest.explain: The grid is a map that helps doctors find where to look.

advancedTest.q: Two textbooks place the same organ in different abdominal regions. The likeliest reason is that they:
choices: Draw the region grid from different surface landmarks
Treat the left and right sides differently
Measured their organs in different decades
Rely on veterinary rather than human anatomy
advancedTest.explain: The nine-region boundaries vary between schemes, for example subcostal vs transpyloric and intertubercular vs interspinous, so region assignment differs.

advancedTest.q: Why does early appendicitis pain start near the umbilicus rather than at the appendix itself?
choices: Visceral pain is felt in the midline by embryonic gut origin
The appendix begins its development near the umbilicus
The umbilicus contains many sensory nerve endings
Inflammation first spreads along the umbilical vessels
advancedTest.explain: Visceral pain follows the embryonic gut level, and the appendix is midgut, so pain is periumbilical. It shifts to the right lower quadrant once the parietal peritoneum is involved.

advancedTest.q: Upright living-subject CT studies challenged classic surface projections mainly because cadaveric data:
choices: Were based on axial rather than coronal sections
Came from supine, embalmed bodies with displaced viscera
Relied on young subjects with minimal variation
Used planes that were defined in Terminologia Anatomica
advancedTest.explain: Viscera sit lower when people are upright and vary with body habitus. Supine embalmed specimens misrepresent the living, standing position.

advancedTest.q: Embryology prefers cranial/caudal over superior/inferior mainly because:
choices: Embryos are mostly studied in transverse section
Cranial structures develop before caudal ones
Superior and inferior were removed from Terminologia Anatomica
The terms stay valid regardless of body posture or species
advancedTest.explain: Cranial/caudal and dorsal/ventral refer to body axes, so they hold for curled embryos and quadrupeds, where superior and inferior break down.

lessons.title: Serous Membranes: Parietal vs Visceral Layers

levels.kid:
Imagine pushing your fist into a soft, floppy balloon. Your fist does not go inside the balloon. Instead, the balloon wraps around it. Now part of the balloon hugs your fist, and part of it faces outward. A thin space is left in between.

Your heart, lungs and tummy organs are wrapped like that fist. Each one sits in a thin, slippery bag called a **serous membrane**. The layer touching the organ is the inside layer. The layer lining the wall of your body is the outside layer.

Between the two layers there is a tiny bit of slippery fluid, like a drop of oil. It lets your heart beat and your lungs puff up without rubbing. Neat, right?
levels.hs:
A **serous membrane** (or **serosa**) is a thin, smooth lining found inside the closed body cavities. It has two continuous layers:

- The **parietal layer** lines the body wall (from Latin *paries*, "wall").
- The **visceral layer** covers the surface of an organ (from *viscera*, "internal organs").

The two layers are one continuous sheet, folded back on itself. Between them is a potential space, the **serous cavity**, which holds only a thin film of **serous fluid**. The fluid acts as a lubricant, so moving organs can slide without friction.

The trunk has three serous membranes:
- **Pleura** around each lung (pleural cavity)
- **Serous pericardium** around the heart (pericardial cavity)
- **Peritoneum** in the abdomen and pelvis (peritoneal cavity)

A helpful model is a fist pushed into a balloon. The organ is the fist. It sits *outside* the cavity, even though it is wrapped by the membrane.

Real example: in **pleurisy**, inflamed pleural layers rub together. Breathing in becomes sharply painful, and a doctor may hear a scratchy **friction rub** through a stethoscope.

The two layers also feel pain differently. The parietal layer senses pain sharply and in a precise spot. The visceral layer is mostly insensitive to cutting or touch.
levels.college:
Every serous membrane consists of a single layer of flat **mesothelium** (simple squamous epithelium of mesodermal origin). It rests on a basement membrane and a thin layer of loose connective tissue, the **subserosa**. Parietal and visceral layers are continuous at a **reflection**, the line where the membrane turns from the wall onto the organ. Examples include the root of the lung, the great vessels at the heart, and the mesenteries.

**The three serosae of the trunk**
- **Pleura**: parietal pleura is named by region (costal, diaphragmatic, mediastinal, cervical). It is continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum. The **pulmonary ligament** is the empty double fold that hangs below the hilum.
- **Serous pericardium**: the parietal layer is fused to the inner surface of the tough **fibrous pericardium**. The visceral layer is the **epicardium**.
- **Peritoneum**: parietal and visceral peritoneum are linked by double-layered **mesenteries**, omenta and ligaments. These carry vessels and nerves to the organs.

**Nerve supply and pain** (high-yield)
- **Parietal layers** take the innervation of the wall they line, through somatic nerves. Pain is sharp and well localized. Costal pleura is supplied by **intercostal nerves**. Central diaphragmatic and mediastinal pleura, and the parietal pericardium, are supplied by the **phrenic nerve (C3 to C5)**, so pain may be **referred to the shoulder**. Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the lower intercostal, subcostal and lumbar nerves.
- **Visceral layers** take the autonomic supply of the organ. They do not respond to cutting, but they do respond to stretch and ischemia. The pain is dull and poorly localized.

This explains the classic course of appendicitis. The pain first spreads vaguely around the umbilicus, from visceral afferents (T10). It then shifts to sharp right iliac fossa pain once the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum.

**Fluid accumulation** turns a potential space into a real one: pleural effusion, pericardial effusion and ascites. Air in the pleural space is a **pneumothorax**.
levels.phd:
Mesothelium is a specialized epithelium that also has mesenchymal features. Mesothelial cells co-express **cytokeratins** and **vimentin**. Their surface carries dense microvilli and secretes **hyaluronan**, phosphatidylcholine-rich **surfactant**, and proteoglycans that form a glycocalyx. As a result, lubrication works by **boundary lubrication** rather than pure fluid-film separation. Mesothelial cells also express **mesothelin**, **calretinin** and **WT1**, which are used as immunohistochemical markers.

**Fluid physiology.** Normal pleural fluid is roughly 0.1 to 0.3 mL/kg per hemithorax, forming a film about 10 to 20 μm thick. Its balance follows the **Starling principle**. Fluid is filtered mainly from **parietal systemic capillaries**, because systemic pressure exceeds bronchial-pulmonary pressure. It drains through **stomata** in the parietal pleura, 2 to 10 μm openings that lead into submesothelial **lacunae** and lymphatics. These stomata are concentrated over the lower mediastinal and diaphragmatic surfaces. Comparable diaphragmatic stomata clear peritoneal fluid. This is why intraperitoneal particles, cells and bacteria drain preferentially through the diaphragm into mediastinal (parasternal) nodes. It also explains why subphrenic collections form.

**Pleural pressure.** The opposing elastic recoil of lung and chest wall creates a subatmospheric pleural pressure of about −3 to −5 cmH₂O at functional residual capacity. In the upright position this pressure has a vertical gradient that is more negative at the apex. The gradient contributes to regional differences in ventilation. The serous coupling transmits chest-wall motion to the lung, and losing it causes collapse.

**Light's criteria (1972)** separate exudates from transudates using fluid-to-serum protein and LDH ratios. Exudates reflect mesothelial or capillary injury, such as infection, malignancy or inflammation. Transudates reflect altered Starling forces, as in heart failure or cirrhosis. The criteria are sensitive but misclassify about 25% of transudates as exudates, especially after diuresis. In such cases a serum-to-effusion albumin gradient greater than 1.2 g/dL helps.

**Repair** has a distinctive pattern. Mesothelial wounds re-epithelialize diffusely across the whole surface at once, not only from the wound edges. The precursor cells may be free-floating mesothelial cells or submesothelial progenitors, which remains debated. Imbalance between fibrinolysis (tPA versus PAI-1) and deposition favors **adhesions**. Mesothelial-to-mesenchymal transition drives fibrosis in long-term **peritoneal dialysis**.
levels.expert:
Several clinical consequences follow from the parietal/visceral distinction and the potential-space concept.

**Exploiting the space.** Pleurodesis deliberately obliterates the pleural space to prevent recurrent pneumothorax or malignant effusion. It can be done chemically, most often with talc, or mechanically by abrasion or pleurectomy. Indwelling pleural catheters are an alternative for malignant effusion, and the AMPLE and TIME2 trials compared the two approaches. Peritoneal dialysis uses the roughly 1 to 2 m² of peritoneum as a semipermeable exchange surface. Encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis is a rare, feared late complication. In hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC), cytotoxic drugs are bathed directly against the serosa after cytoreduction for peritoneal surface malignancy.

**Spread along serosae.** Transcoelomic metastasis follows peritoneal fluid flow toward the pouch of Douglas, the right paracolic gutter and the subphrenic spaces. Ovarian and gastric cancers are typical, and the Krukenberg pattern and omental cake are classic findings. **Malignant mesothelioma** is strongly linked to amphibole asbestos exposure, with a latency of decades. Loss of **BAP1** on immunohistochemistry and **CDKN2A** deletion help distinguish it from reactive mesothelial hyperplasia. Combined nivolumab and ipilimumab (CheckMate 743) improved survival in unresectable pleural disease, especially in non-epithelioid histology.

**Pitfalls**
- Shoulder-tip pain can come from diaphragmatic irritation, such as subphrenic blood, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or post-laparoscopy CO₂ (Kehr's sign). It is easy to misattribute to the shoulder itself.
- Pericarditis pain that eases on leaning forward and worsens on lying flat reflects parietal irritation. Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression reflects epicardial inflammation of the subjacent myocardium.
- Tamponade depends on how fast the fluid accumulates, because the fibrous pericardium is relatively stiff. Under 200 mL gathered acutely can be lethal, while slowly accumulating effusions can exceed a litre.
- A "dry" tap can mean that adhesions have made the potential space disappear.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Ventriculoperitoneal shunts rely on peritoneal absorption of CSF. Peritoneal adhesions, pseudocysts or ascites can cause distal shunt failure, and ventriculopleural or ventriculoatrial routes are then alternatives.

**Open questions** include the identity of the mesothelial progenitor cell, whether anti-adhesion barriers and fibrinolytic strategies actually reduce small-bowel obstruction, and the role of peritoneal immune aggregates in tumour tolerance. Milky spots are omental lymphoid clusters with their own resident **GATA6⁺ cavity macrophages**.

keyPoints: Serous membranes have a parietal (wall) and visceral (organ) layer that are continuous
Between the layers is a potential space holding a thin lubricating film of serous fluid
The trunk has three serosae: pleura, serous pericardium and peritoneum
Parietal layers have somatic nerves: sharp, well-localized pain
Visceral layers have autonomic nerves: dull, poorly localized pain from stretch or ischemia
Fluid or air can turn the potential space into a real one (effusion, ascites, pneumothorax)

test.q: Which layer of a serous membrane covers the surface of an organ?
test.explain: Visceral comes from viscera, the internal organs. The parietal layer lines the body wall.

test.q: What normally occupies the serous cavity between the two layers?
test.explain: The serous cavity is a potential space holding only a lubricating film. Air there would be a pneumothorax.

test.q: The epicardium is another name for the:
test.explain: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium on the heart surface is the epicardium.

test.q: Pain from the costal parietal pleura is carried by which nerves?
test.explain: Parietal layers share the somatic supply of the wall they line. The costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves.

test.q: Irritation of the central diaphragmatic pleura is often felt in the shoulder because it is supplied by:
choices: The phrenic nerve, C3 to C5
test.explain: The phrenic nerve shares spinal segments with the skin of the shoulder, so the pain is referred there.

test.q: Visceral serous layers mainly respond to which stimulus?
test.explain: Visceral layers are insensitive to cutting but sense stretch and ischemia, which produces dull, poorly localized pain.

test.q: In appendicitis, pain shifts to the right iliac fossa when the appendix irritates the:
test.explain: Early periumbilical pain is visceral. Sharp, localized pain begins once the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum is irritated.

test.q: Which cell type lines all serous membranes?
test.explain: Serosae are lined by mesothelium, a simple squamous epithelium of mesodermal origin.

test.q: Fluid collecting in the peritoneal cavity is called:
test.explain: Ascites is free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. Hemothorax and empyema involve the pleural space.

test.q: The line where a serous membrane turns from the body wall onto an organ is called a ___.
test.explain: At reflections the parietal and visceral layers are continuous, for example at the lung root.

test.q: What is the name of the serous membrane that lines the abdominal cavity?
test.explain: The peritoneum lines the abdominopelvic cavity and covers many abdominal organs.

test.q: Air in the pleural space is called a ___.
test.explain: Air breaks the serous coupling between lung and chest wall, so the lung collapses.

kidTest.q: What does a serous membrane wrap around?
kidTest.explain: Slippery serous bags wrap the heart, lungs and tummy organs.

kidTest.q: What is between the two layers?
choices: A tiny bit of slippery fluid
kidTest.explain: A drop of slippery fluid lets the organs move smoothly.

kidTest.q: Why is the fluid helpful?
kidTest.explain: Like oil, it lets the heart and lungs move without rubbing.

kidTest.q: In the balloon model, what is your fist like?
kidTest.explain: The fist is the organ, wrapped by the balloon.

kidTest.q: The serous bag is like a floppy b _ _ _ _ _ _ wrapped around a fist.
kidTest.explain: A fist pushed into a balloon shows how the two layers wrap an organ.

advancedTest.q: Why does intraperitoneal fluid, along with cells and bacteria, tend to reach mediastinal lymph nodes?
choices: Omental fat filters it straight into the thoracic duct
Diaphragmatic stomata drain it into lacunae and lymphatics
Mesenteric lymph flows upward without passing any nodes
Visceral peritoneal capillaries absorb it into the portal vein
advancedTest.explain: Parietal stomata are concentrated over the diaphragm and connect to lymphatics that drain toward mediastinal nodes.

advancedTest.q: After diuresis, a heart failure effusion meets Light's criteria for an exudate. What is the best next step?
choices: Repeat Light's criteria using glucose levels
Treat it as malignant until cytology returns
advancedTest.explain: Light's criteria misclassify some transudates, especially after diuresis. An albumin gradient above 1.2 g/dL supports a transudate.

advancedTest.q: A slowly growing litre-sized pericardial effusion is tolerated, while a small acute bleed causes tamponade. Why?
choices: The visceral layer absorbs fluid faster in slow effusions
The stiff fibrous pericardium stretches when loaded slowly
Blood has a higher osmotic pressure than serous fluid
Slow effusions drain through pericardial stomata
advancedTest.explain: Rate matters. The relatively stiff fibrous sac adapts to gradual stretch, but it cannot accommodate a sudden volume increase.

advancedTest.q: Which finding best separates mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial hyperplasia?
advancedTest.explain: Calretinin, WT1 and vimentin mark mesothelium in general. BAP1 loss and CDKN2A deletion support malignancy.

lessons.title: Embryonic Folding and Formation of the Body Cavities

levels.kid:
When you were tiny, before you were born, you started out as a flat little disc, like a pancake made of cells.

Then something amazing happened. The pancake **folded**. The front edge curled down, the back edge curled down, and the two sides rolled toward each other, like wrapping a burrito.

Inside the burrito, a long tube formed. That tube became your gut, the path food travels through.

A hollow space also got trapped inside. This space is called a **cavity**. Later, a wall called the **diaphragm** grew across it like a shelf. The top part holds your heart and lungs. The bottom part holds your stomach and intestines.

So your chest and belly spaces come from one big fold!
levels.hs:
Early in development, around the third week, the embryo is a flat **trilaminar disc** with three layers: **ectoderm** (outer), **mesoderm** (middle) and **endoderm** (inner). During week 3 a split opens inside the side part of the mesoderm, called the **lateral plate mesoderm**. It divides into two sheets:
- **Somatic (parietal) mesoderm**, which lines the body wall.
- **Splanchnic (visceral) mesoderm**, which wraps the gut.

The gap between them is the **intraembryonic coelom**, the future body cavity.

In **week 4** the disc folds in two directions:
- **Lateral folding**: the sides roll down and meet in the midline, closing the ventral body wall and pinching the endoderm into the **gut tube**.
- **Head-to-tail (cephalocaudal) folding**: the head and tail ends curl under. This swings the developing heart and a thick block of mesoderm called the **septum transversum** from in front of the head down into the future chest.

At first the coelom is one continuous horseshoe-shaped space. Partitions then divide it into the **pericardial cavity** (around the heart), two **pleural cavities** (around the lungs) and the **peritoneal cavity** (around the abdominal organs).

Real example: if the sides fail to close properly, organs can develop outside the body wall. This is seen in birth defects like **gastroschisis**.
levels.college:
**Origin of the coelom.** In week 3, small spaces open in the lateral plate mesoderm and merge into the horseshoe-shaped **intraembryonic coelom**. The pericardial part sits cranially, in front of the oropharyngeal membrane. Its two limbs run caudally and at first open laterally into the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity). Somatic mesoderm plus ectoderm forms the **somatopleure**, which becomes the body wall. Splanchnic mesoderm plus endoderm forms the **splanchnopleure**, which becomes the gut wall. This is why every serous cavity has a lining derived from somatic mesoderm and an organ covering derived from splanchnic mesoderm.

**Folding (week 4).**
- **Lateral folding** brings the somatopleure together ventrally, closing the body wall except at the **umbilical ring**. Endoderm is enclosed as foregut, midgut and hindgut. The midgut stays connected to the yolk sac by the **vitelline (omphaloenteric) duct**.
- **Cephalocaudal folding** rotates the cardiogenic area and the **septum transversum** ventrally and caudally. The heart ends up in the thorax, with the septum transversum lying caudal to it.
- The midgut is suspended from the posterior wall by the **dorsal mesentery**, a double layer of splanchnic mesoderm. A ventral mesentery exists only in the region of the foregut.

**Partitioning.**
- The **septum transversum** partly separates the pericardial and peritoneal cavities. It leaves dorsal openings, the **pericardioperitoneal canals**, which are the future pleural cavities.
- **Pleuropericardial membranes** grow in and fuse, sealing the pericardial cavity off from the pleural cavities. They carry the phrenic nerves and become the **fibrous pericardium**.
- **Pleuroperitoneal membranes** close the canals caudally, the left side closing later than the right.

**The diaphragm** has four sources:
- the septum transversum (central tendon)
- the pleuroperitoneal membranes
- the dorsal mesentery of the esophagus (crura)
- muscle from the body wall at the periphery

Because the septum transversum formed at cervical levels C3-C5, the phrenic nerve keeps that cervical origin.
levels.phd:
**Mechanics of folding.** Folding is driven mainly by differential growth. The neural tube and somites expand rapidly while the amnion-yolk sac junction lags behind. The yolk sac becomes relatively constricted, and the embryo bulges into the amniotic cavity. Ventral body wall closure depends on the lateral body folds converging. Mouse genetics point to roles for **Tfap2a**, **Bmp** signaling and **Pitx2**, and defects in this process are implicated in ventral wall defects. The classic lateral fold model has also been refined. Lineage studies suggest that most of the definitive ventral wall musculature arrives secondarily by hypaxial myoblast migration from somites into somatic mesoderm. The folds only provide a primary body wall, a scaffold of somatopleure and connective tissue.

**Coelomic epithelium.** The lining of the coelom becomes **mesothelium**. Beyond lining the cavities, it is an active progenitor tissue. **Epicardium**, derived from the proepicardial organ at the septum transversum, undergoes epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to give coronary smooth muscle and cardiac fibroblasts. In a similar way, coelomic mesothelium contributes to the hepatic stellate cells and to the gonadal somatic lineages.

**Septum transversum as signaling hub.** Hepatic endoderm (the liver diverticulum) grows into the septum transversum. There, **FGF** from cardiac mesoderm and **BMP4** from the septum induce hepatic fate. Septum-derived mesenchyme supplies the liver's sinusoidal stroma. The dorsal part of the septum is left behind as the central tendon and as the ventral mesogastrium (lesser omentum, falciform ligament).

**Pleuroperitoneal folds (PPFs).** Older textbooks portrayed the PPFs as passive membrane flaps. Work by Kardon and colleagues (Merrell et al., 2015, Nature Genetics) showed instead that PPF fibroblasts are the source of muscle connective tissue and guide the migration of myogenic precursors into the diaphragm. Mosaic loss of **Gata4** in PPF fibroblasts produced localized weak muscle-free regions that herniated. This gives a mechanistic model for **congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH)**, in which the defect starts in connective tissue, not muscle.

**Asymmetry.** Closure of the left pericardioperitoneal canal lags behind the right. Together with the protective liver on the right, this explains why most CDH is a left posterolateral **Bochdalek** hernia.

Disrupting retinoic acid signaling (the nitrofen rat model, vitamin A-deficiency studies) reproduces CDH, implicating the RA pathway.
levels.expert:
**Clinical translation of coelomic partitioning.**
- **CDH** occurs in roughly 1 in 3,000-4,000 live births. Herniation during the pseudoglandular stage compresses both lungs, producing ipsilateral and contralateral pulmonary hypoplasia with abnormal, muscularized pulmonary vasculature. The persistent pulmonary hypertension that follows, not the hole itself, drives mortality.
- **Prenatal assessment** uses the observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (O/E LHR) on ultrasound, MRI lung volumetry, and the position of the liver. Liver herniated above the diaphragm predicts a worse outcome.
- In the **TOTAL trials** (Deprest et al., NEJM 2021), fetoscopic endoluminal tracheal occlusion (FETO) improved survival in severe left CDH. The trapped lung fluid stretches the lungs and promotes their growth. The benefit was smaller in moderate cases and came with a higher risk of preterm birth. Patient selection remains debated.

**Ventral wall defects as folding failures.**
- **Omphalocele**: the midgut fails to return from physiological umbilical herniation. The sac is covered by amnion and peritoneum. It is strongly associated with aneuploidy (trisomy 13 and 18) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, so karyotyping and a search for associated anomalies are mandatory.
- **Gastroschisis**: a paraumbilical defect, usually to the right of the cord, with no covering sac. It is usually an isolated finding linked to young maternal age. Its cause is still disputed: theories include vascular disruption of the right umbilical vein or omphalomesenteric artery, versus failed lateral fold fusion. The exposed bowel is damaged by contact with amniotic fluid.
- **Pentalogy of Cantrell** combines a supraumbilical omphalocele, a sternal cleft, an anterior diaphragmatic defect from failure of the septum transversum, a pericardial defect and ectopia cordis. In effect, it is a failure of the cephalic fold.

**Pitfalls and pearls.**
- **Morgagni hernias** are anterior retrosternal or parasternal defects that are often found incidentally in adults. Do not confuse them with Bochdalek hernias.
- Shoulder-tip pain from subdiaphragmatic irritation reflects the cervical (C3-C5) origin of the phrenic nerve. This cervical supply is also why high cervical cord injury compromises breathing.
- The coelom's early continuity is why peritoneal-pleural communications occur. For example, ascites can track into the chest through diaphragmatic defects (hepatic hydrothorax), usually on the right side.

**Open questions.** It remains uncertain why the connective-tissue lineage fails in the pleuroperitoneal folds in human CDH. Two strategies are under investigation: whether antenatal stimulation of lung growth works better through tracheal occlusion or through pharmacological strategies such as sildenafil or RA-pathway modulation, and whether mesothelial progenitors could be harnessed for regeneration.

keyPoints: The lateral plate mesoderm splits into somatic and splanchnic layers around the intraembryonic coelom
Lateral folding closes the body wall and encloses the gut tube
Head-to-tail folding moves the heart and septum transversum into the chest
Pleuropericardial and pleuroperitoneal membranes divide the coelom into separate cavities
The diaphragm forms from four sources; the phrenic nerve keeps its C3-C5 origin
Incomplete closure causes CDH (usually a left Bochdalek hernia), omphalocele and gastroschisis

lessons.title: Fascial Layers of the Thoracic and Abdominal Walls

levels.kid:
Think about an onion. When you cut it, you see layer after layer, each one wrapped neatly around the next. Your body wall is built a bit like that.

Under your skin there is a soft, squishy layer with some fat in it. Under that are your muscles. Every muscle is wrapped in a thin, tough sheet, a bit like plastic wrap around a sandwich. These wrapping sheets are called **fascia** (say "FASH-ee-uh").

Inside the muscles there is one more wrapper that lines the whole inside of your chest and belly. It works like the lining inside a coat.

Surgeons need to know every layer. When they operate, they count the layers as they go through, so they always know exactly where they are.
levels.hs:
**Fascia** is connective tissue that wraps, separates and supports body structures. The walls of the chest (thorax) and belly (abdomen) are built in layers, and they follow a similar pattern from outside to inside:

- **Skin**
- **Superficial fascia** (subcutaneous tissue): loose tissue containing fat, small vessels and nerves
- **Deep fascia**: thin sheets that cover the muscles
- **Muscle layers**
- **Endothoracic fascia** in the chest, or **transversalis fascia** in the abdomen: the inner lining of the wall
- **Extraperitoneal fat** (in the abdomen)
- **Parietal pleura** or **parietal peritoneum**: the serous lining of the cavity

In the lower abdomen, the superficial fascia splits into two named layers. **Camper's fascia** is the outer, fatty layer. **Scarpa's fascia** is the deeper, membranous layer. It is thinner but tougher, and surgeons stitch it when they close an incision.

These layers are not just labels. They form **planes**, which are natural boundaries where fluid, blood or infection can spread, and where surgeons can separate tissues with little bleeding.

A real example: if the urethra tears below the pelvic floor, urine can leak into the space under Scarpa's fascia. Because of how these layers attach, the urine can travel up the lower abdominal wall but cannot pass down into the thighs.
levels.college:
The thoracic and abdominal walls share one layered plan, with regional specializations.

**Thoracic wall** (outside to inside): skin, superficial fascia (which contains the breast), deep fascia over pectoralis major (**pectoral fascia**), the chest muscles, then the ribs with three intercostal muscle layers. These are the external intercostal, the internal intercostal and the innermost intercostal. The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, from top to bottom) run in the costal groove, between the internal and innermost layers. Inside the ribs lies the **endothoracic fascia**, which separates the wall from the costal parietal pleura. Above the first rib it thickens into the **suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia)**, which covers the cervical pleura.

**Anterolateral abdominal wall** (outside to inside):
- Skin
- **Camper's fascia**: the fatty layer, which continues with superficial fat elsewhere
- **Scarpa's fascia**: the membranous layer, which fuses with the fascia lata about a fingerbreadth below the inguinal ligament
- Investing (deep) fascia over the external oblique
- External oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis, with their aponeuroses forming the **rectus sheath**
- **Transversalis fascia**
- **Extraperitoneal fat**
- **Parietal peritoneum**

Key continuities:
- In the perineum, Scarpa's fascia continues as **Colles' fascia** (the superficial perineal fascia). Over the penis it continues as the superficial (dartos) fascia, and in the scrotum as the **dartos fascia** with smooth muscle.
- The transversalis fascia is one part of a continuous **endoabdominal fascia**, named by the muscle it covers: diaphragmatic, psoas and iliac fascia.
- The **deep inguinal ring** is an opening in the transversalis fascia. The spermatic cord's **internal spermatic fascia** comes from this layer.

Clinically, the potential space deep to Scarpa's and Colles' fascia explains how fluid spreads after a straddle injury that ruptures the bulbous urethra. The fluid can extend into the scrotum, the penis and the anterior abdominal wall, but not into the thighs (because of the fusion with the fascia lata) or back into the anal triangle (because of the attachment to the perineal membrane).
levels.phd:
Fascia is no longer treated as passive packing. Current terminology (from the Federative International Programme for Anatomical Terminology and the Fascia Research Congress) separates several categories. **Superficial fascia** is the membranous layer within the subcutis. **Deep (investing) fascia** is either aponeurotic, made of collagen sheets in layers with different fiber directions, or epimysial, tightly bound to the muscle. **Visceral and parietal fasciae** line the body cavities. Much of the debate about naming in the abdomen comes from the fact that "layers" are really zones where loose and dense connective tissue grade into each other.

**Subcutaneous architecture.** Microdissection by Lancerotto and colleagues described the subcutis as two fat layers separated by a true membranous layer. In the **superficial adipose tissue**, large fat lobules sit between vertical retinacula cutis. In the **deep adipose tissue**, flatter lobules sit between oblique, loosely arranged septa. Camper's and Scarpa's "fasciae" therefore correspond to the superficial fat layer and to the membranous layer. Scarpa's layer is well defined in the lower abdomen but thins out over the upper abdomen and thorax.

**Transversalis fascia** is the parietal layer of the endoabdominal fascia. Below the arcuate line it lies directly against the rectus abdominis, because all the aponeuroses pass in front of the muscle there. It contributes to the **iliopubic tract** and, below the inguinal ligament, to the anterior wall of the **femoral sheath**. Whether it has a separate "posterior lamina" is still debated. Some surgical anatomists describe a two-layer transversalis fascia with the inferior epigastric vessels running between the layers. Others call the deeper layer the **preperitoneal (urogenital) fascia**, which also wraps the kidneys and ureters as part of a continuous retroperitoneal fascial system.

**Endothoracic fascia** is the matching thoracic layer. It is thin over the ribs, more defined where it is reinforced by transversus thoracis, and continuous through the diaphragm's openings with the endoabdominal fascia. This continuity explains why, in rare cases, extrapleural collections can track between the two cavities.

**Mechanobiology.** Deep fascia contains fibroblasts, telocyte-like cells and abundant free nerve endings, including nociceptors. Hyaluronan between its sublayers lets the layers slide over each other. Changes in this gliding have been proposed as a cause of myofascial pain, although the evidence remains mixed and largely comes from ultrasound and correlation studies.
levels.expert:
For the clinician, the fascial planes of the trunk wall matter mainly as working spaces and as routes along which disease spreads.

**Regional anesthesia.** Fascial plane blocks rely on spread of local anesthetic within a defined layer under ultrasound guidance:
- The **transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block** places anesthetic between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, where the T7 to L1 anterior rami run.
- The **rectus sheath block** targets the space behind the rectus muscle.
- The **quadratus lumborum** and **erector spinae plane (ESP)** blocks work further back. How far the ESP block spreads into the paravertebral and epidural spaces, and therefore whether it relieves visceral pain, is still debated. Cadaver dye studies and clinical results do not fully agree.
- In the chest, the **PECS I/II** and **serratus anterior plane** blocks use the pectoral and serratus fascial planes for breast and chest wall surgery.

A known pitfall is that the injected solution spreads unpredictably, so the extent of numbness can vary from patient to patient.

**Hernia surgery.** Laparoscopic TEP and TAPP repairs work in the **preperitoneal space** behind the transversalis fascia. Surgeons enter the space of Retzius (behind the pubis) and the space of Bogros (to the side). Two danger zones guide safe mesh fixation:
- The **triangle of doom**, bounded by the vas deferens and the gonadal vessels, over the external iliac vessels
- The **triangle of pain**, containing the lateral femoral cutaneous and genitofemoral nerves

Opening the wrong plane, for example going in front of the transversalis fascia, causes bleeding and poor mesh position.

**Abdominal wall closure.** Approximating Scarpa's layer may reduce seroma and dead space. The evidence is modest, and practice varies between surgeons.

**Necrotizing soft tissue infection.** Infection can spread rapidly along the superficial fascial plane, for example in **Fournier's gangrene**, which tracks through the Colles'–dartos–Scarpa's continuum. Skin findings can lag behind the underlying tissue death, so early surgical exploration takes priority over waiting for imaging.

**Open questions.** Several issues remain unsettled:
- The real architecture of the transversalis and preperitoneal fascia
- Which nerve and blood vessel structures run in which plane
- Whether fascial "densification" is a reproducible cause of pain

High-resolution ultrasound, elastography and 3D histological reconstruction are actively reshaping how we think about the fascial planes of the trunk wall.

For neurosurgery, the same thinking applies at the spine. Thoracolumbar fascia and paraspinal planes govern muscle-sparing approaches and ESP analgesia after spinal fusion.

keyPoints: Trunk walls follow one plan: skin, superficial fascia, deep fascia, muscle, inner fascia, cavity lining
Lower abdominal superficial fascia has fatty Camper's and membranous Scarpa's layers
Scarpa's continues as Colles' and dartos fascia and fuses with fascia lata below the inguinal ligament
Transversalis fascia (abdomen) and endothoracic fascia (thorax) line the inner wall, outside the serous membrane
Intercostal VAN runs between internal and innermost intercostals
Fascial planes guide spread of fluid and infection and are used for nerve blocks and hernia repair

They hold most of the body's red blood cells

lessons.title: Surface Landmarks and Vertebral Levels (Sternal Angle, Transpyloric Plane)

levels.kid:
Your body has secret map marks you can feel through your skin. Doctors use them like street signs to find things hidden inside.

Run your finger down from the dip at the bottom of your neck. You will feel a little bump on your breastbone. That bump is called the **sternal angle**. It is like a big sign that says "Second rib here!" Doctors start counting ribs from that spot.

Lower down, halfway between the top of your breastbone and the top of your pubic bone, is an invisible line. Many important tummy parts sit near it, like the exit door of your stomach.

The bones of your back line up with these marks too. So by feeling the outside, a doctor can picture the inside!
levels.hs:
A **surface landmark** is a bump, groove or line you can see or feel on the body that tells you where a deeper structure lies. Anatomists also match landmarks to **vertebral levels**, written as letters plus numbers: T4 means the fourth thoracic vertebra, L1 the first lumbar.

Key landmarks of the trunk:
- **Jugular (suprasternal) notch**: the dip at the top of the sternum, roughly level with T2/T3.
- **Sternal angle (angle of Louis)**: the ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. The second rib's cartilage attaches here, so it is the starting point for counting ribs. It lines up with the disc between T4 and T5.
- **Xiphisternal joint**: near T9.
- **Transpyloric plane (of Addison)**: a horizontal line halfway between the jugular notch and the top of the pubic symphysis, at about L1. It crosses the pylorus, the tips of the 9th costal cartilages and the hila of the kidneys.
- **Subcostal plane**: the lowest edge of the ribcage (10th costal cartilage), about L3.
- **Supracristal plane**: across the tops of the iliac crests, about L4. It is used for lumbar punctures.

Real example: to listen to the heart's valves or insert a chest drain, a clinician finds the sternal angle, slides onto rib 2, then counts down the intercostal spaces. That is safer than guessing.
levels.college:
Surface anatomy links palpable features to deep structures and vertebral levels. Levels are averages in a supine adult; they shift with posture, breathing and body habitus.

**The sternal angle (T4/T5 disc)** is the trunk's most important horizontal reference. A plane through it (the thoracic plane) marks:
- The division between superior and inferior mediastinum
- The beginning and end of the aortic arch
- The tracheal bifurcation (carina), approximately, in the supine cadaver
- The azygos vein arching over the right main bronchus into the SVC
- The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking under the arch
- The ligamentum arteriosum and the pulmonary trunk bifurcation
- Rib 2 articulating laterally, the starting point for counting ribs

**Other thoracic levels.** The jugular notch is at T2/T3. The xiphisternal joint is at T9. Diaphragmatic openings follow "I 8 10 Eggs At 12": IVC at T8, esophagus at T10, aortic hiatus at T12.

**Abdominal planes.**
- **Transpyloric plane (L1)**: lies midway between the jugular notch and the pubic symphysis, or about a hand's breadth below the xiphoid. It runs near the pylorus, the duodenojejunal flexure, the neck of the pancreas, the fundus of the gallbladder (where the right linea semilunaris meets the costal margin), the renal hila, the 9th costal cartilages, the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the end of the spinal cord (conus medullaris, L1/L2) in adults.
- **Subcostal plane (L3)**: the inferior margin of the 10th costal cartilage. It lies near the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery and the third part of the duodenum.
- **Umbilicus**: about L3/L4, dermatome T10.
- **Supracristal plane (L4)**: the iliac crest tops. It marks the aortic bifurcation and serves as a lumbar puncture landmark.
- **Intertubercular plane (L5)**: the tubercles of the iliac crests.

The subcostal and intertubercular planes, together with the midclavicular lines, divide the abdomen into nine regions.
levels.phd:
Most classic vertebral level tables come from cadaver dissection, where the body is supine, embalmed and has no muscle tone. Imaging in living subjects shows systematic differences. Mirjalili and colleagues used CT in living adults (Clinical Anatomy, around 2012) and reported the following:
- The sternal angle usually lay at T4/T5, but the range was wide.
- The carina was more often lower, around T5 to T6, than at the sternal angle.
- The aortic arch summit was usually above the plane.
- The SVC/right atrial junction and the azygos termination also varied.

In the same work, the **transpyloric plane** most often lay at L1 or L2. However, the pylorus itself lay on the plane in only a minority of subjects. The stomach and pylorus descend substantially in the upright posture, often to L3 or below. The renal hila, pancreatic neck and SMA origin sat near the plane but scattered over a full vertebral level or more.

The transpyloric plane was introduced by Christopher Addison in the late 1890s as a reproducible skeletal reference. Its value is as a ruler (half the jugulo-pubic distance), not as a guarantee that the pylorus lies there.

Several factors drive this variation:
- **Posture**: viscera fall when standing.
- **Respiration**: the diaphragm moves several centimetres between full inspiration and expiration.
- **Age**: kyphosis and loss of disc height change the levels.
- **Habitus**: obesity raises the diaphragm.
- **Sex**
- **Vertebral numbering anomalies**: lumbosacral transitional vertebrae occur in a meaningful minority of people.

The adult conus medullaris ends most often near L1/L2, with a normal range from about T12 to L3. A line between the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) usually crosses L4 or L4/L5. Palpation, however, often places it a level higher than imaging does, especially in obese patients.

The practical conclusion is that vertebral levels are probability distributions, not fixed points. Updated reference values now appear in modern textbooks, and the field continues to debate whether teaching should replace cadaveric numbers with living-imaging ranges.
levels.expert:
Clinically, landmarks are starting estimates that you then confirm. This matters most where an error of one level changes outcomes.

- **Rib counting and chest drains.** Count from the sternal angle at rib 2, not from the costal margin. The lower ribs are hard to feel and the 12th rib can be short or absent. Drains go in the "triangle of safety": anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a line at about the 5th intercostal space, with the apex below the axilla. Insert just above a rib to spare the neurovascular bundle. Ultrasound is increasingly standard.
- **Neuraxial procedures.** Tuffier's line from palpation can sit a level high. Combined with conus variation, this is why lumbar puncture targets L3/L4 or L4/L5. Pre-procedural ultrasound improves level identification, particularly in obese patients.
- **Spine surgery.** Wrong-level surgery remains a recognized never-event, and transitional anatomy is a common contributor. Intraoperative fluoroscopy, counting consistently from C2 or the sacrum, and correlation with preoperative full-spine imaging reduce the risk. Neurosurgeons should document the counting method in the record. For thoracic lesions without clear landmarks, a marker such as a fiducial placed before surgery is often used.
- **Central lines and imaging.** The carina is a common radiographic surrogate for the cavoatrial junction when checking catheter tip position. This works because the carina is a more reliable landmark than the sternal angle on a chest film.
- **Abdominal examination.** Murphy's point (right linea semilunaris at the costal margin) estimates the gallbladder fundus. Liver span is percussed in the midclavicular line, and both shift with respiration and posture.

Open questions: How should variability be taught without losing useful heuristics? Can AI-based automatic vertebral labelling on CT and MRI reliably handle transitional anatomy? And how far should procedural training move from palpation toward routine point-of-care ultrasound?

keyPoints: Sternal angle = rib 2 = T4/T5 disc; start rib counting here
The thoracic plane marks superior/inferior mediastinum and aortic arch ends
Transpyloric plane lies at L1, halfway from jugular notch to pubic symphysis
Subcostal plane ~L3, supracristal ~L4 (lumbar puncture landmark)
Diaphragm openings: IVC T8, esophagus T10, aorta T12
Living imaging shows levels vary with posture, breathing and anatomy

test.q: Which rib's cartilage articulates at the sternal angle?
test.explain: Rib 2 joins at the manubriosternal joint, which makes the sternal angle the reference point for counting ribs.

test.q: The sternal angle lies at roughly which vertebral level?
test.explain: It lies at the T4/T5 disc. T2/T3 is the jugular notch and T9 is the xiphisternal joint.

test.q: The plane through the sternal angle separates which two regions?
test.explain: The thoracic plane divides the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum.

test.q: How is the transpyloric plane defined?
choices: Halfway from jugular notch to pubis
Across the tops of the iliac crests
At the lowest edge of the bony ribcage
test.explain: Addison's plane lies halfway between the jugular notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis, at about L1.

test.q: Which structure lies near the transpyloric plane?
test.explain: The renal hila sit near L1. The aortic bifurcation is at L4, the IMA origin is near L3 and the carina is in the thorax.

test.q: The supracristal plane at about L4 is used mainly as a landmark for:
test.explain: The tops of the iliac crests guide lumbar puncture below the end of the spinal cord.

test.q: The esophagus passes through the diaphragm at about:
test.explain: Remember 'I 8 10 Eggs At 12': IVC at T8, esophagus at T10, aorta at T12.

test.q: Why do clinicians count ribs downward from the sternal angle?
choices: Lower ribs are hard to feel reliably
test.explain: The lower ribs are hard to palpate and the 12th can be short. The sternal angle reliably identifies rib 2.

test.q: The subcostal plane passes through the lower margin of which costal cartilage?
test.explain: The subcostal plane runs along the inferior margin of the 10th costal cartilage, at about L3.

test.q: The sternal angle is also called the angle of ___.
test.explain: It is the angle of Louis, the joint between the manubrium and the sternal body.

test.q: What vertebral level does the transpyloric plane classically mark? (letter and number)
test.explain: The transpyloric plane is classically at L1.

test.q: The dip at the top of the sternum is the jugular, or supra___, notch.
test.explain: The suprasternal (jugular) notch lies at about T2/T3.

kidTest.q: What is the sternal angle?
kidTest.explain: It is a small ridge you can feel on your breastbone.

kidTest.q: Doctors use the sternal angle to start counting what?
kidTest.explain: It marks the second rib, so counting ribs starts there.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors use bumps they can feel?
kidTest.explain: Bumps on the outside act like signs showing where inside parts are.

kidTest.q: Which stomach part sits near the invisible tummy line?
kidTest.explain: The exit of the stomach, the pylorus, is near that line.

kidTest.q: The bones of your back that line up with the marks are called v _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Back bones are vertebrae, and doctors match marks to them.

advancedTest.q: CT studies of living adults found the carina usually:
choices: Above the sternal angle at T3
At the level of the xiphoid
advancedTest.explain: Living imaging places the carina lower than cadaveric teaching, around T5 to T6, because embalmed supine bodies differ from living ones.

advancedTest.q: Why is the pylorus often well below the transpyloric plane in a standing patient?
choices: The kidneys push the stomach down
The plane rises with spinal flexion
advancedTest.explain: Upright posture lets the stomach sag, often to L3 or lower. Inspiration actually lowers the diaphragm rather than raising it.

advancedTest.q: Lumbar puncture targets L3/L4 or L4/L5 mainly because:
choices: The aorta bifurcates at the L3 vertebra
The iliac crests lie precisely at the L5 level
Conus may reach L2; palpation reads high
The dura ends exactly at the L2 level
advancedTest.explain: The conus ranges down to about L2/L3, and palpated Tuffier's line often lies a level higher than true, so lower spaces add a safety margin.

advancedTest.q: A key cause of wrong-level spine surgery is:
choices: Counting from the sacrum on imaging
advancedTest.explain: Transitional vertebrae change the numbering. The other options are methods that reduce errors rather than cause them.
